# Reference palette

This is the **reference instance** of the data-viz method: every parameter the
method needs, filled in with a validated default palette. The rest of the skill
is system-agnostic - **to target your brand, substitute this file's values** and
re-run the validator. Nothing else changes.

## How to use these values

Everything below is plain hex. In an HTML chart, **define the slots you use as
CSS custom properties in a local `<style>` block** at the top of the file, then
reference them by role throughout - so the light/dark values swap in one place,
and the chart body is written against roles rather than raw hex:

```css
.viz-root {
  color-scheme: light;
  --surface-1:      #fcfcfb;   /* chart surface */
  --text-primary:   #0b0b0b;
  --text-secondary: #52514e;
  --series-1:       #2a78d6;   /* categorical slot 1 */
  /* ...only the roles this chart uses */
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:where(:not([data-theme="light"])) .viz-root {
    color-scheme: dark;
    --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
    --text-primary:   #f0efec;
    --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
    --series-1:       #3987e5;
  }
}
:root[data-theme="dark"] .viz-root {
  color-scheme: dark;
  --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
  --text-primary:   #f0efec;
  --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
  --series-1:       #3987e5;
}
```

Declare the dark values under both scopes as above - the media query covers
the OS setting; the `data-theme` scope covers the viewer's theme toggle,
which must win both ways (the `:not(...)` guard lets a light stamp beat
OS-dark; `:where()` keeps the media block below the toggle scope).

## Categorical palette

Both modes are selected. The dark column is the same eight hues stepped for the
dark surface, not a separate palette:

| Slot | Hue | Light | Dark |
|------|-----|-------|------|
| 1 | blue | `#2a78d6` | `#3987e5` |
| 2 | orange | `#eb6834` | `#d95926` |
| 3 | aqua | `#1baf7a` | `#199e70` |
| 4 | yellow | `#eda100` | `#c98500` |
| 5 | magenta | `#e87ba4` | `#d55181` |
| 6 | green | `#008300` | `#008300` |
| 7 | violet | `#6250d6` | `#9085e9` |
| 8 | red | `#e34948` | `#e66767` |

This order passes every hard gate in both modes on the default *adjacent*
pairlist (stacks, bars, lines): worst adjacent CVD Delta E 9.1 light / 8.4 dark
(OKLab ×100, >=8 target), worst adjacent normal-vision Delta E 19.6 light / 19.3
dark (>=15 floor). Under `--pairs all` (scatter, bubble, choropleth, small
multiples) the full eight cannot clear the floors - with all 28 pairs in
play no ordering can (the pairlist no longer depends on order), and
re-stepping is off the table by the documented-palette rule - so those
chart forms carry a series cap: **the first three slots validate all-pairs
in both modes** (worst pair CVD Delta E 9.2 light / 9.4 dark, normal-vision 24.0
light / 20.9 dark - clear of the CVD warn band). Past three, fold to "Other" or
facet: the fourth slot puts yellow and orange on screen
together, and that pair fails the all-pairs floors (normal-vision 13.7
light; CVD 4.8 dark). Three light-mode slots (magenta, yellow, aqua)
sit below 3:1 contrast on the light surface: the **relief rule** applies (ship
visible direct labels or the table view). The dark steps were chosen for the
dark band (OKLCH L ~ 0.48-0.67, >= 3:1 on the dark surface) and validated as a
set. (Ordering history: adopted July 2026 for its more harmonious opening -
the same eight hues and steps as its predecessor, re-ordered, zero hex
changes. The predecessor validated its first FOUR slots all-pairs, with its
dark run in the 6-8 CVD warn band, so secondary encoding was required there;
this order deliberately trades that fourth slot - yellow now sits beside orange -
for better-looking leading colors. Revisit the trade if yellow<->orange
confusion shows up in real charts with four or more series; undoing it is a
pure re-order. Light slot 7 has since been lightened, `#4a3aa7` -> `#6250d6`
(August 2026); the adjacent-pair figures above are unchanged by that move, the
non-adjacent blue<->violet pair now sits below both floors under `--pairs all`
(normal-vision 10.5, CVD 4.5 - inside the range the series cap already
excludes), and the order enumeration was run with the earlier value.) When you
swap in your own ramps, hold your palette to the full gate.

The slot **ordering** is the CVD-safety mechanism, not cosmetic - candidate
orderings were enumerated and only those clearing every adjacent gate in both
modes kept (see `color-formula.md` § Themes); this default is one of the
passing orders, picked among them for its opening colors. When you swap in
your brand's hues, do the same: run the validator on candidate orderings and
choose only among the passing ones.

## Sequential hue

Default single hue: **blue**, light->dark. When two sequential contexts appear at
once, the second takes the next categorical slot's hue (orange), each as its own
one-hue ramp.

| step | hex | step | hex | step | hex | step | hex |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | `#cde2fb` | 250 | `#86b6ef` | 400 | `#3987e5` | 550 | `#1c5cab` |
| 150 | `#b7d3f6` | 300 | `#6da7ec` | 450 | `#2a78d6` | 600 | `#184f95` |
| 200 | `#9ec5f4` | 350 | `#5598e7` | 500 | `#256abf` | 650 | `#104281` |
| | | | | | | 700 | `#0d366b` |

The full 100->700 range is for **sequential** encoding (continuous magnitude -
heatmaps, choropleths) where the lightest step means "near zero" and is allowed
to recede toward the surface. For an **ordinal** ramp (discrete ordered marks -
funnel stages, tiers - validated with `--ordinal`), the step nearest the surface
must still clear 2:1: on light, start no lighter than **step 250** (`#86b6ef`,
2.06:1); on dark, go no darker than **step 600** (`#184f95`, 2.15:1).

## Diverging pair

**blue <-> red** - warm/cool poles that read as opposite. Neutral midpoint is gray
(light `#f0efec`, dark `#383835`). Equal step count per arm. (blue<->aqua was
rejected - both cool, the midpoint doesn't read as "nothing".)

## Status palette (fixed - never themed)

| role | hex | light-surface contrast | dark-surface contrast |
|---|---|---|---|
| good | `#0ca30c` | 3.27 | 5.19 |
| warning | `#fab219` | 1.79 | 9.49 |
| serious | `#ec835a` | 2.57 | 6.60 |
| critical | `#d03b3b` | 4.68 | 3.62 |

Dark: same four steps - all clear 3:1 on the dark surface (`#1a1a19`) and remain
distinct from the dark categorical slots. On the light surface, warning and
serious are sub-3:1 by design; the **icon + label** pairing is the mitigation, so
a status color never carries meaning alone. These steps are deliberately distinct
from the categorical slots so a status color never impersonates a series -
distinct enough that nothing collides at a glance, not enough for hue to
carry the distinction unaided: measured by the series floor's own bar
(unsimulated Delta E >= 15), around nine categorical-vs-status pairs per mode sit
below 15 - in light mode red vs critical and yellow vs warning both measure
4.8, slot-2 orange sits 5.8 from status-serious, and the light success text
green `#006300` sits 10.1 from the series green; green vs status-good (9.7)
holds in both modes, since both hexes are mode-invariant. The rule is general: any series color beside a
same-hue-family status or delta cue leans on the icon + label pairing and on
placement; never on hue alone.

## Texture fill (the accessibility channel)

One hand-drawn **"Lines"** fill, used at **45° and its 135° mirror only**. Inked
tone-on-tone (a darker step of the fill's own ramp). On value scales it is
*ordered* (rotation steps with magnitude; arm angle carries the diverging sign).
Triggered by the accessibility setting, print, or `forced-colors` - never
decorative, never on by default.

## Surfaces (for the validator)

- Light chart surface: `#fcfcfb`
- Dark chart surface: `#1a1a19`

These are the validator's built-in defaults. **When you swap in your own
palette, re-run against your own surfaces:**
`--surface <your-light> --mode light` and `--surface <your-dark> --mode dark` -
contrast and band results are only meaningful against the surface the chart
actually renders on.

## Chart chrome & ink

| Role | Light | Dark |
|---|---|---|
| Chart surface | `#fcfcfb` | `#1a1a19` |
| Page plane | `#f9f9f7` | `#0d0d0d` |
| Primary ink | `#0b0b0b` | `#f0efec` |
| Secondary ink | `#52514e` | `#c3c2b7` |
| Muted (axis/labels) | `#898781` | `#898781` |
| Gridline (hairline) | `#e1e0d9` | `#2c2c2a` |
| Baseline / axis | `#c3c2b7` | `#383835` |
| Delta up good (success text) | `#006300` | `#0ca30c` |
| Border (hairline ring) | `rgba(11,11,11,0.10)` | `rgba(255,255,255,0.10)` |

## Filter controls

Filters are standard UI, not chart components - the chart layer only adds the
composition rules in `interaction.md`. A date-range control is a list of preset
rows (today, last 7/30/90 days, month-to-date) with selection marked by a 16px
bold check, hover as a ghost wash, and custom range behind a hairline in the
footer. Dimension filters are a standard combobox.

## Typeface & figures

Everything - including the hero figure - stays in the system sans: `system-ui,
-apple-system, "Segoe UI", sans-serif`. No display or serif face anywhere. Large
standalone numbers (hero figure, stat-tile values) use the default proportional
figures; reserve `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for columns that must align
vertically (table rows, axis ticks). Substitute your brand's UI sans here.
# Marks & anatomy

The quiet, considered look is a few fixed specs plus two pieces of negative space.
The data is the only thing allowed to be loud.

## Mark specs (fixed across every chart)

| Mark | Spec |
|---|---|
| Bar / column | **<= 24px thick** (cap it - never fill the slot; let the band's leftover be air); **4px rounded data-end, square at the baseline**; grows from a single baseline |
| Line | **2px**, round join/cap |
| Marker / end-dot | **>= 8px** (r >= 4), filled with the series color |
| Area fill | the series hue at **~10% opacity** (a wash, never a saturated block) |
| Gridlines / axes | one-step-off-surface gray, **hairline (1px), solid** (never dashed), recessive |

## The two spacers (white doing the separating)

- **Surface gap.** A **2px gap** in the surface color separates touching marks - every
  segment of a stacked bar, and every adjacent (touching) bar, the same width. Keep it
  one consistent width across a stack; neighbors one step apart read distinct because of
  the gap, not a stroke drawn around them.
- **Surface ring.** Dots and end-markers carry a **2px ring in the surface color**,
  so they stay legible where they cross a line or overlap each other. The ring is part
  of the mark's hover/hit target, not just spacing - see `interaction.md` (small dots
  are easy to under-size for hover).

Never draw a border around a mark to separate it. The gap and the ring are the
mechanism; a stroke adds data-weight ink that isn't data.

## Labels & legend

A **legend is always present for two or more series** - the dependable identity
channel; never make the reader rely on color-matching alone. Direct labels then ride
the marks to *supplement* it. **A single series needs no legend box**: there is only
one color, so the chart's title or subtitle already says what is plotted. A box with
one swatch restates the title and costs space.

- **Label selectively - never a number on every point.** A value beside every dot or
  segment is chaos and goes unread. Label the endpoint, the extreme, or the one series
  the story is about; let the axis, the legend, and the tooltip/table carry the rest.
  Direct labels work *because* they are sparing - flood the chart and they stop working.
- **Direct labels before gridlines; gridlines before a second axis.**
- **A label that won't fit doesn't get clipped - measure first.** Only place a label
  *inside* a bar or stacked segment when the rendered text fits with comfortable
  padding on both sides. If it doesn't fit: for a whole bar/column, move the label
  outside the bar end (or to the tooltip if there's no room outside either); for an
  *interior* stacked segment (which has no free end),
  skip the inline label and let the legend + tooltip carry it. Either way the value
  stays in the table view, so nothing is gated. Never use `overflow: hidden` on the
  segment to "solve" it - that crops the first/last characters and is worse than no
  label. Text never overflows or is clipped by its own mark.
- Bars -> value at the tip. Columns -> value on the cap. Lines -> value at the end.
- Y-axis ticks: round to clean numbers, compact from 1,000 up (0 / 1K / 2K); they
  carry the values you didn't directly label, so keep them unless every value is labeled.
- **Text never wears the data color.** Marks - bars, lines, dots, area fills - carry
  the series color; labels, values, legends, and axis text use **text tokens**
  (primary / secondary / muted). A light categorical hue (yellow, aqua) is illegible
  as text on the surface. Identity comes from the colored mark *beside* the text - a
  dot, a short line-key, a swatch - never from coloring the text itself. A label set
  *inside* a colored fill (a stacked segment, a map tile) is the one exception: pick
  white or ink by the fill's luminance so it always clears contrast.
- **When end-labels collide, don't stack them.** Direct end-labels work when series
  separate at the right edge. When lines converge, nudging labels apart vertically
  detaches them from their lines and reads as noise - instead use **leader lines**
  (a thin connector from label to line-end), facet into **small multiples**, or fall
  back to the legend + tooltip. Past ~4 converging series, small multiples is usually right.

## Figures - when the form is a number

- **Stat tile** contract: `label` (sentence case, no trailing colon) · `value` (Sans
  semibold, auto-compact: 1,284 / 12.9K / $4.2M) · `delta` (optional; signed,
  vs a named period; color = direction × whether up is good) · `trend` (optional;
  12-point sparkline in the de-emphasis hue, current period in the accent).
- **Meter:** the fill carries severity (accent -> warning -> danger); the unfilled
  track is a **lighter step of the same ramp** (blue-on-blue, etc.) so state reads
  across the whole bar.
- **Hero figure.** The single number a dashboard leads with, >=48px, in the same
  sans as everything else (never a display or serif face - it reads as off-brand
  decoration). Exactly one per view.
- **Proportional figures for big numbers; tabular only in columns.** A large
  standalone value (hero figure, stat-tile value) uses the font's default
  proportional figures - `tabular-nums` gives every digit the width of a `0`, so a
  number like `121` looks loose at display sizes. Reserve
  `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for columns of numbers that must align
  vertically (table rows, axis ticks).

## Texture - the backup channel (opt-in)

Where hue fails - full-severity CVD, grayscale print, `forced-colors` - texture
carries identity. One directional hand-drawn fill, used at **45° and its 135° mirror
only** (never horizontal/vertical - those read as gridlines/bars). Inked tone-on-tone
(a step from the fill's own ramp), equal loudness across slots. On value scales the
texture is *ordered* (rotation steps with magnitude; arm angle carries the diverging
sign) so it never misstates the value. Triggered by an accessibility setting, print,
or `forced-colors` - never on by default. (See `palette.md`.)

```css
    --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
    --text-primary:   #f0efec;
    --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
    --series-1:       #3987e5;
  }
}
:root[data-theme="dark"] .viz-root {
  color-scheme: dark;
  --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
  --text-primary:   #f0efec;
  --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
  --series-1:       #3987e5;
}
```

Declare the dark values under both scopes as above - the media query covers
the OS setting; the `data-theme` scope covers the viewer's theme toggle,
which must win both ways (the `:not(...)` guard lets a light stamp beat
OS-dark; `:where()` keeps the media block below the toggle scope).

## Categorical palette

Both modes are selected. The dark column is the same eight hues stepped for the
dark surface, not a separate palette:

| Slot | Hue | Light | Dark |
|------|-----|-------|------|
| 1 | blue | `#2a78d6` | `#3987e5` |
| 2 | orange | `#eb6834` | `#d95926` |
| 3 | aqua | `#1baf7a` | `#199e70` |
| 4 | yellow | `#eda100` | `#c98500` |
| 5 | magenta | `#e87ba4` | `#d55181` |
| 6 | green | `#008300` | `#008300` |
| 7 | violet | `#6250d6` | `#9085e9` |
| 8 | red | `#e34948` | `#e66767` |

This order passes every hard gate in both modes on the default *adjacent*
pairlist (stacks, bars, lines): worst adjacent CVD Delta E 9.1 light / 8.4 dark
(OKLab ×100, >=8 target), worst adjacent normal-vision Delta E 19.6 light / 19.3
dark (>=15 floor). Under `--pairs all` (scatter, bubble, choropleth, small
multiples) the full eight cannot clear the floors - with all 28 pairs in
play no ordering can (the pairlist no longer depends on order), and
re-stepping is off the table by the documented-palette rule - so those
chart forms carry a series cap: **the first three slots validate all-pairs
in both modes** (worst pair CVD Delta E 9.2 light / 9.4 dark, normal-vision 24.0
light / 20.9 dark - clear of the CVD warn band). Past three, fold to "Other" or
facet: the fourth slot puts yellow and orange on screen
together, and that pair fails the all-pairs floors (normal-vision 13.7
light; CVD 4.8 dark). Three light-mode slots (magenta, yellow, aqua)
sit below 3:1 contrast on the light surface: the **relief rule** applies (ship
visible direct labels or the table view). The dark steps were chosen for the
dark band (OKLCH L ~ 0.48-0.67, >= 3:1 on the dark surface) and validated as a
set. (Ordering history: adopted July 2026 for its more harmonious opening -
the same eight hues and steps as its predecessor, re-ordered, zero hex
changes. The predecessor validated its first FOUR slots all-pairs, with its
dark run in the 6-8 CVD warn band, so secondary encoding was required there;
this order deliberately trades that fourth slot - yellow now sits beside orange -
for better-looking leading colors. Revisit the trade if yellow<->orange
confusion shows up in real charts with four or more series; undoing it is a
pure re-order. Light slot 7 has since been lightened, `#4a3aa7` -> `#6250d6`
(August 2026); the adjacent-pair figures above are unchanged by that move, the
non-adjacent blue<->violet pair now sits below both floors under `--pairs all`
(normal-vision 10.5, CVD 4.5 - inside the range the series cap already
excludes), and the order enumeration was run with the earlier value.) When you
swap in your own ramps, hold your palette to the full gate.

The slot **ordering** is the CVD-safety mechanism, not cosmetic - candidate
orderings were enumerated and only those clearing every adjacent gate in both
modes kept (see `color-formula.md` § Themes); this default is one of the
passing orders, picked among them for its opening colors. When you swap in
your brand's hues, do the same: run the validator on candidate orderings and
choose only among the passing ones.

## Sequential hue

Default single hue: **blue**, light->dark. When two sequential contexts appear at
once, the second takes the next categorical slot's hue (orange), each as its own
one-hue ramp.

| step | hex | step | hex | step | hex | step | hex |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | `#cde2fb` | 250 | `#86b6ef` | 400 | `#3987e5` | 550 | `#1c5cab` |
| 150 | `#b7d3f6` | 300 | `#6da7ec` | 450 | `#2a78d6` | 600 | `#184f95` |
| 200 | `#9ec5f4` | 350 | `#5598e7` | 500 | `#256abf` | 650 | `#104281` |
| | | | | | | 700 | `#0d366b` |

The full 100->700 range is for **sequential** encoding (continuous magnitude -
heatmaps, choropleths) where the lightest step means "near zero" and is allowed
to recede toward the surface. For an **ordinal** ramp (discrete ordered marks -
funnel stages, tiers - validated with `--ordinal`), the step nearest the surface
must still clear 2:1: on light, start no lighter than **step 250** (`#86b6ef`,
2.06:1); on dark, go no darker than **step 600** (`#184f95`, 2.15:1).

## Diverging pair

**blue <-> red** - warm/cool poles that read as opposite. Neutral midpoint is gray
(light `#f0efec`, dark `#383835`). Equal step count per arm. (blue<->aqua was
rejected - both cool, the midpoint doesn't read as "nothing".)

## Status palette (fixed - never themed)

| role | hex | light-surface contrast | dark-surface contrast |
|---|---|---|---|
| good | `#0ca30c` | 3.27 | 5.19 |
| warning | `#fab219` | 1.79 | 9.49 |
| serious | `#ec835a` | 2.57 | 6.60 |
| critical | `#d03b3b` | 4.68 | 3.62 |

Dark: same four steps - all clear 3:1 on the dark surface (`#1a1a19`) and remain
distinct from the dark categorical slots. On the light surface, warning and
serious are sub-3:1 by design; the **icon + label** pairing is the mitigation, so
a status color never carries meaning alone. These steps are deliberately distinct
from the categorical slots so a status color never impersonates a series -
distinct enough that nothing collides at a glance, not enough for hue to
carry the distinction unaided: measured by the series floor's own bar
(unsimulated Delta E >= 15), around nine categorical-vs-status pairs per mode sit
below 15 - in light mode red vs critical and yellow vs warning both measure
4.8, slot-2 orange sits 5.8 from status-serious, and the light success text
green `#006300` sits 10.1 from the series green; green vs status-good (9.7)
holds in both modes, since both hexes are mode-invariant. The rule is general: any series color beside a
same-hue-family status or delta cue leans on the icon + label pairing and on
placement; never on hue alone.

## Texture fill (the accessibility channel)

One hand-drawn **"Lines"** fill, used at **45° and its 135° mirror only**. Inked
tone-on-tone (a darker step of the fill's own ramp). On value scales it is
*ordered* (rotation steps with magnitude; arm angle carries the diverging sign).
Triggered by the accessibility setting, print, or `forced-colors` - never
decorative, never on by default.

## Surfaces (for the validator)

- Light chart surface: `#fcfcfb`
- Dark chart surface: `#1a1a19`

These are the validator's built-in defaults. **When you swap in your own
palette, re-run against your own surfaces:**
`--surface <your-light> --mode light` and `--surface <your-dark> --mode dark` -
contrast and band results are only meaningful against the surface the chart
actually renders on.

## Chart chrome & ink

| Role | Light | Dark |
|---|---|---|
| Chart surface | `#fcfcfb` | `#1a1a19` |
| Page plane | `#f9f9f7` | `#0d0d0d` |
| Primary ink | `#0b0b0b` | `#f0efec` |
| Secondary ink | `#52514e` | `#c3c2b7` |
| Muted (axis/labels) | `#898781` | `#898781` |
| Gridline (hairline) | `#e1e0d9` | `#2c2c2a` |
| Baseline / axis | `#c3c2b7` | `#383835` |
| Delta up good (success text) | `#006300` | `#0ca30c` |
| Border (hairline ring) | `rgba(11,11,11,0.10)` | `rgba(255,255,255,0.10)` |

## Filter controls

Filters are standard UI, not chart components - the chart layer only adds the
composition rules in `interaction.md`. A date-range control is a list of preset
rows (today, last 7/30/90 days, month-to-date) with selection marked by a 16px
bold check, hover as a ghost wash, and custom range behind a hairline in the
footer. Dimension filters are a standard combobox.

## Typeface & figures

Everything - including the hero figure - stays in the system sans: `system-ui,
-apple-system, "Segoe UI", sans-serif`. No display or serif face anywhere. Large
standalone numbers (hero figure, stat-tile values) use the default proportional
figures; reserve `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for columns that must align
vertically (table rows, axis ticks). Substitute your brand's UI sans here.
# Marks & anatomy

The quiet, considered look is a few fixed specs plus two pieces of negative space.
The data is the only thing allowed to be loud.

## Mark specs (fixed across every chart)

| Mark | Spec |
|---|---|
| Bar / column | **<= 24px thick** (cap it - never fill the slot; let the band's leftover be air); **4px rounded data-end, square at the baseline**; grows from a single baseline |
| Line | **2px**, round join/cap |
| Marker / end-dot | **>= 8px** (r >= 4), filled with the series color |
| Area fill | the series hue at **~10% opacity** (a wash, never a saturated block) |
| Gridlines / axes | one-step-off-surface gray, **hairline (1px), solid** (never dashed), recessive |

## The two spacers (white doing the separating)

- **Surface gap.** A **2px gap** in the surface color separates touching marks - every
  segment of a stacked bar, and every adjacent (touching) bar, the same width. Keep it
  one consistent width across a stack; neighbors one step apart read distinct because of
  the gap, not a stroke drawn around them.
- **Surface ring.** Dots and end-markers carry a **2px ring in the surface color**,
  so they stay legible where they cross a line or overlap each other. The ring is part
  of the mark's hover/hit target, not just spacing - see `interaction.md` (small dots
  are easy to under-size for hover).

Never draw a border around a mark to separate it. The gap and the ring are the
mechanism; a stroke adds data-weight ink that isn't data.

## Labels & legend

A **legend is always present for two or more series** - the dependable identity
channel; never make the reader rely on color-matching alone. Direct labels then ride
the marks to *supplement* it. **A single series needs no legend box**: there is only
one color, so the chart's title or subtitle already says what is plotted. A box with
one swatch restates the title and costs space.

- **Label selectively - never a number on every point.** A value beside every dot or
  segment is chaos and goes unread. Label the endpoint, the extreme, or the one series
  the story is about; let the axis, the legend, and the tooltip/table carry the rest.
  Direct labels work *because* they are sparing - flood the chart and they stop working.
- **Direct labels before gridlines; gridlines before a second axis.**
- **A label that won't fit doesn't get clipped - measure first.** Only place a label
  *inside* a bar or stacked segment when the rendered text fits with comfortable
  padding on both sides. If it doesn't fit: for a whole bar/column, move the label
  outside the bar end (or to the tooltip if there's no room outside either); for an
  *interior* stacked segment (which has no free end),
  skip the inline label and let the legend + tooltip carry it. Either way the value
  stays in the table view, so nothing is gated. Never use `overflow: hidden` on the
  segment to "solve" it - that crops the first/last characters and is worse than no
  label. Text never overflows or is clipped by its own mark.
- Bars -> value at the tip. Columns -> value on the cap. Lines -> value at the end.
- Y-axis ticks: round to clean numbers, compact from 1,000 up (0 / 1K / 2K); they
  carry the values you didn't directly label, so keep them unless every value is labeled.
- **Text never wears the data color.** Marks - bars, lines, dots, area fills - carry
  the series color; labels, values, legends, and axis text use **text tokens**
  (primary / secondary / muted). A light categorical hue (yellow, aqua) is illegible
  as text on the surface. Identity comes from the colored mark *beside* the text - a
  dot, a short line-key, a swatch - never from coloring the text itself. A label set
  *inside* a colored fill (a stacked segment, a map tile) is the one exception: pick
  white or ink by the fill's luminance so it always clears contrast.
- **When end-labels collide, don't stack them.** Direct end-labels work when series
  separate at the right edge. When lines converge, nudging labels apart vertically
  detaches them from their lines and reads as noise - instead use **leader lines**
  (a thin connector from label to line-end), facet into **small multiples**, or fall
  back to the legend + tooltip. Past ~4 converging series, small multiples is usually right.

## Figures - when the form is a number

- **Stat tile** contract: `label` (sentence case, no trailing colon) · `value` (Sans
  semibold, auto-compact: 1,284 / 12.9K / $4.2M) · `delta` (optional; signed,
  vs a named period; color = direction × whether up is good) · `trend` (optional;
  12-point sparkline in the de-emphasis hue, current period in the accent).
- **Meter:** the fill carries severity (accent -> warning -> danger); the unfilled
  track is a **lighter step of the same ramp** (blue-on-blue, etc.) so state reads
  across the whole bar.
- **Hero figure.** The single number a dashboard leads with, >=48px, in the same
  sans as everything else (never a display or serif face - it reads as off-brand
  decoration). Exactly one per view.
- **Proportional figures for big numbers; tabular only in columns.** A large
  standalone value (hero figure, stat-tile value) uses the font's default
  proportional figures - `tabular-nums` gives every digit the width of a `0`, so a
  number like `121` looks loose at display sizes. Reserve
  `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for columns of numbers that must align
  vertically (table rows, axis ticks).

## Texture - the backup channel (opt-in)

Where hue fails - full-severity CVD, grayscale print, `forced-colors` - texture
carries identity. One directional hand-drawn fill, used at **45° and its 135° mirror
only** (never horizontal/vertical - those read as gridlines/bars). Inked tone-on-tone
(a step from the fill's own ramp), equal loudness across slots. On value scales the
texture is *ordered* (rotation steps with magnitude; arm angle carries the diverging
sign) so it never misstates the value. Triggered by an accessibility setting, print,
or `forced-colors` - never on by default. (See `palette.md`.)

content.text:
The mockup is open in your browser. It's a clickable page, `docs/mockups/scorecard_explorer_mockup.html`, and every number in it comes from the live Scorecard API (FY25 snapshot dated 2026-04-10). The conversation replies are scripted, not real LLM answers; a banner at the top of the page says so.

**What you can try**

*Outcomes page*
- All 15 tiles show live figures: achieved of expected (for example, Energy: 214.5M of 575.6M, 37%), a progress bar, and a small trend line for the related context indicator.
- You can filter tiles by vertical and sort them by "Furthest from expected".
- Ask "Biggest gaps". The answer ranks the three areas furthest from their expected results (FCV 30%, Climate resilience 32%, Connected Communities 34%) and highlights those tiles. Every number has a ✓ you can hover to see its source.
- Ask "Energy access in Western Africa". It opens the Energy page already filtered to that region.

*Explorer page* (click any tile)
- Filters at the top for institution, area, sex and snapshot, plus a line saying what's currently shown.
- **What this shows:** a short summary of the current view in which every number is verified, including figures we compute such as gaps and ratios.
- **Client context:** a trend chart comparing all countries with the selected region.
- **WBG results:** achieved vs expected, viewable by region, by institution or across snapshots (FY24→FY26). Energy also has a map view.
- **Ask the Scorecard:** try the suggestion chips:
  - "girls in western africa" sets the filters and offers undo.
  - "compare to eastern and southern africa" returns an answer card, a chart, a "How I got this" section and a "Pin to canvas" button.
  - "which regions lag most?" ranks the regions.
  - "what does expected mean?" explains the term.
- ◐ in the header switches between light and dark.

**Data issues the pipeline will have to handle**
- Water, Gender and Jobs have no single total. Their results come only broken into sub-indicators, and the mockup shows the largest one.
- Private capital *enabled* has an expected value but no achieved value.
- The map only covers World Bank projects that are tied to a specific country (34 countries, about 40M people). That's much less than the 214.5M total, which also includes IFC and MIGA. We'd need to label the map clearly or drop it.

**Design points to react to**
1. Is the split screen (charts on the left, conversation on the right) the right balance, or should the conversation take more space?
2. On tiles, should "% of expected" stay the main visual, or would you rather lead with the achieved figure only?
3. Keep the map despite its limited coverage, or drop it?
4. Keep the look neutral and editorial as it is now, or move closer to the World Bank's colours, without copying its branding?

Comment in the chat or edit the template directly. The template is `docs/mockups/mockup_template.html` and the data is in `mock_data.json` next to it. I'll rebuild the page after any change.

content: We're building a Django Scorecard Explorer with an LLM assistant for your World Bank assessment (Q1 and Q3), and the interactive UI mockup is open in your browser. Next, review it and tell me your answers to the four design questions.

content.text:
I've reworked the mockup with your three changes and reopened it in your browser (`docs/mockups/scorecard_explorer_mockup.html`).

**1. Landing page cut down to the live site's tile style.** Each tile now has only an icon (coloured by vertical), a short title with the key word in bold ("**Students** supported with better education"), the achieved figure large, the expected figure below it, and a small paired bar comparing the two. I removed the context lines, the percentage labels, the footnote, the subtitle and the outcome-name line. The page is now a title, the Ask bar, three example questions, the vertical filters and the tiles.

**2. A map on the indicator page, as on the live site.** The results panel opens on a country map with an **Achieved / Expected** toggle. You can switch to By region, By institution or Over time.
- Choosing a region zooms the map to it. Choosing a country zooms to its region and outlines the country.
- Clicking a country on the map sets the Area filter, and the chat logs the change with an undo option.
- The Area filter now lists the regions, fragile & conflict-affected states, and every country with results (172 areas in total).
- Try "Students supported in Ghana" from the landing page: it opens No Learning Poverty filtered to Ghana, showing **3.9M of 8.8M** students supported and the map zoomed to Western & Central Africa.

**3. Light mode only.** I removed the dark theme and the toggle.

**One correction you should know about:** the live site shows the **FY26 snapshot (2026-10-11)**, while the mockup had been on FY25. I re-pulled the data, and the landing figures now match your screenshot exactly: 282M / 339M, 327M / 439M, 615M / 742M, 21 / 31. The app will default to the latest snapshot.

**Data gaps the pipeline and app will need to handle:**
- **Learning poverty for Ghana:** there's no country value. The context chart shows Western & Central Africa instead and says "no data for Ghana".
- **Jobs and private capital mobilized:** neither has an all-countries figure, so their tiles show only the title.

**How the files fit together:**
- `mockup_template.html` is the design.
- `mock_data.json` holds the FY26 data pulled from the API.
- `build_mockup.py` merges the two into the page you open. Re-run it after editing the template.

What would you like to change next? Otherwise, if the layout is close enough, I'll start the data pipeline and turn this mockup into the Django templates.

# Vision: Voice & Video Explainers for the Scorecard (exploratory, beyond the brief) > Status: **concept / plan only**. Not part of the Q1 requirements. The mockup (`docs/mockups/`) includes a working > *preview* (🎬 "Explain with video" and 🎤 voice input), built with the browser's own speech APIs in place of a real > generated presenter. ## 1. The idea Make the Scorecard feel like a conversation with a knowledgeable analyst, not a dashboard: - **Watch:** "Explain this view" produces a 60–90 second narrated explainer: a presenter (avatar or voice-only) walks through the current selection, scene by scene, with the charts animating in sync. - **Ask:** at any point, the user can ask a follow-up **by voice or text** ("why is South Asia lower?"). The answer comes back spoken and on screen, grounded in the same verified data. - **Accessible by default:** captions, transcripts, and audio-first answers for users with low literacy or visual impairments, plus multilingual narration for a global audience. ## 2. How it would work ```mermaid flowchart LR V[Current view
outcome + filters] --> I[Insight builder
verified claims only] I --> SC[Script writer LLM
scenes + narration
claim-tagged] SC --> VER[PCN verifier
every spoken number ✓] VER --> TTS[Text-to-speech
voice + language] VER --> SB[Storyboard
scene → chart spec] TTS --> AV{Presenter mode} AV -->|voice-only| P1[Audio + animated charts
cheapest, instant] AV -->|pre-rendered avatar| P2[Avatar video API
render + cache per view] AV -->|live avatar| P3[Streaming avatar
real-time Q&A] SB --> PL[Player: presenter + synced charts + captions] P1 --> PL P2 --> PL P3 --> PL U[User follow-up
voice or text] --> STT[Speech-to-text] --> R[Same router + tools
as the chat] R --> SC ``` **Key principle: the script is built only from verified claims.** The same Proof-Carrying Numbers check that guards chat answers runs on the narration script *before* any audio or video is generated. A presenter can never say a number that isn't traceable to a source row. Each scene stores its claim IDs, so captions show ✓ links too. ### Three presenter modes (progressive cost and complexity) | Mode | What the user gets | How | Latency | Cost driver | |---|---|---|---|---| | **1. Voice + animated charts** | Narration over charts that change scene by scene, with captions | TTS API (or browser speech, as in the mockup) | ~1–3 s to start (streamed) | TTS characters, very low | | **2. Pre-rendered presenter video** | A talking-head presenter beside the charts | Avatar video API renders the script; **cached** per (outcome, filters, snapshot) | Minutes to render; instant when cached | Per-second of rendered video | | **3. Live interactive presenter** | Real-time spoken Q&A with an avatar | Streaming avatar + speech-to-speech model with **the same tools** as the chat | ~1–2 s per turn | Per-minute streaming session | **Recommended path:** ship **Mode 1** first (cheap, fast, fully grounded). Pre-render **Mode 2** only for the ~15 outcome-area overviews per snapshot (a fixed, cacheable set). Pilot **Mode 3** later for events and briefings. ### Voice Q&A - **Simple pipeline:** speech-to-text → the existing router + tools + verifier → text-to-speech. It reuses everything already built, so it's predictable and verifiable. - **Speech-to-speech realtime models** (single socket, lower latency, support tool calling) are the alternative for Mode 3. The tools stay the same; the verifier still checks the transcript before the answer is shown as text. ## 3. Options landscape (to verify at build time; prices change often) | Need | Options | Notes | |---|---|---| | Avatar video (pre-rendered) | HeyGen API, Synthesia, D-ID, VEED Fabric | HeyGen publishes per-second API rates; Synthesia API access is tied to higher/enterprise tiers | | Live / streaming avatar | HeyGen LiveAvatar, D-ID agents, Tavus | Priced per credit/minute; concurrency limits apply | | Speech-to-speech / realtime voice | OpenAI Realtime (`gpt-realtime`), ElevenLabs agents, Deepgram Voice Agent, Microsoft Voice Live | Support tool calling; compare on latency, interruption handling, languages | | TTS / STT (pipeline) | Any major TTS/STT provider; the browser Web Speech API for prototypes | The mockup uses the browser APIs (no keys, no cost) | Sources: [HeyGen: avatar APIs 2026](https://www.heygen.com/blog/best-ai-avatar-talking-head-apis) · [HeyGen vs Synthesia vs D-ID](https://www.heygen.com/blog/heygen-vs-synthesia-vs-d-id) · [VEED: best avatar APIs](https://www.veed.io/learn/best-avatar-apis) · [Kompozy comparison](https://kompozy.io/ai-video-generation/avatar-video-comparison) · [OpenAI: introducing gpt-realtime](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-realtime/) · [AssemblyAI: realtime API alternatives](https://assemblyai.com/blog/openai-realtime-api-alternatives). Several of these are vendor-authored; treat prices and latency claims as indicative. ## 4. Guardrails specific to voice & video - **Grounding:** narration = verified claims only; scripts that fail verification are not rendered. - **Disclosure:** a visible "AI-generated presenter" label and a watermark on every video; no likeness of real staff without explicit consent; a stock or illustrated presenter by default. - **Accessibility:** captions always on; downloadable transcript; audio descriptions of charts. - **Languages:** narration in the user's language, with numbers formatted for that locale (still verified against the source values). - **Cost control:** cache by (outcome, filters, snapshot, language); render on demand only for popular views; per-session limits for live mode. - **Privacy:** voice audio is not stored by default; transcripts are kept only for the session. ## 5. Phased plan | Phase | Scope | Effort (indicative) | |---|---|---| | 0. Prototype (done in mockup) | Script from verified insights, scenes synced to charts, browser TTS + speech input | — | | 1. Voice explainers | Server-side TTS, streamed audio, captions, 3–5 languages; voice questions via STT → existing pipeline | ~1–2 weeks | | 2. Presenter videos | Avatar API rendering for the 15 outcome overviews per snapshot; CDN caching; disclosure labels | ~2–3 weeks | | 3. Live presenter | Streaming avatar + realtime voice with the same tools; pilot for briefings | ~4+ weeks + vendor review | ## 6. How to evaluate it Comprehension (quick quiz after viewing vs reading), time-to-insight, completion rate, follow-up question rate, verified-number rate in narration (target 100%), latency to first audio, and cost per explainer view.

# Vision: Voice & Video Explainers for the Scorecard (exploratory, beyond the brief) > Status: **concept / plan only**. Not part of the Q1 requirements. The mockup (`docs/mockups/`) includes a working > *preview* (🎬 "Explain with video" and 🎤 voice input), built with the browser's own speech APIs in place of a real > generated presenter. ## 1. The idea Make the Scorecard feel like a conversation with a knowledgeable analyst, not a dashboard: - **Watch:** "Explain this view" produces a 60–90 second narrated explainer: a presenter (avatar or voice-only) walks through the current selection, scene by scene, with the charts animating in sync. - **Ask:** at any point, the user can ask a follow-up **by voice or text** ("why is South Asia lower?"). The answer comes back spoken and on screen, grounded in the same verified data. - **Accessible by default:** captions, transcripts, and audio-first answers for users with low literacy or visual impairments, plus multilingual narration for a global audience. ## 2. How it would work ```mermaid flowchart LR V[Current view
outcome + filters] --> I[Insight builder
verified claims only] I --> SC[Script writer LLM
scenes + narration
claim-tagged] SC --> VER[PCN verifier
every spoken number ✓] VER --> TTS[Text-to-speech
voice + language] VER --> SB[Storyboard
scene → chart spec] TTS --> AV{Presenter mode} AV -->|voice-only| P1[Audio + animated charts
cheapest, instant] AV -->|pre-rendered avatar| P2[Avatar video API
render + cache per view] AV -->|live avatar| P3[Streaming avatar
real-time Q&A] SB --> PL[Player: presenter + synced charts + captions] P1 --> PL P2 --> PL P3 --> PL U[User follow-up
voice or text] --> STT[Speech-to-text] --> R[Same router + tools
as the chat] R --> SC ``` **Key principle: the script is built only from verified claims.** The same Proof-Carrying Numbers check that guards chat answers runs on the narration script *before* any audio or video is generated. A presenter can never say a number that isn't traceable to a source row. Each scene stores its claim IDs, so captions show ✓ links too. ### Three presenter modes (progressive cost and complexity) | Mode | What the user gets | How | Latency | Cost driver | |---|---|---|---|---| | **1. Voice + animated charts** | Narration over charts that change scene by scene, with captions | TTS API (or browser speech, as in the mockup) | ~1–3 s to start (streamed) | TTS characters, very low | | **2. Pre-rendered presenter video** | A talking-head presenter beside the charts | Avatar video API renders the script; **cached** per (outcome, filters, snapshot) | Minutes to render; instant when cached | Per-second of rendered video | | **3. Live interactive presenter** | Real-time spoken Q&A with an avatar | Streaming avatar + speech-to-speech model with **the same tools** as the chat | ~1–2 s per turn | Per-minute streaming session | **Recommended path:** ship **Mode 1** first (cheap, fast, fully grounded). Pre-render **Mode 2** only for the ~15 outcome-area overviews per snapshot (a fixed, cacheable set). Pilot **Mode 3** later for events and briefings. ### Voice Q&A - **Simple pipeline:** speech-to-text → the existing router + tools + verifier → text-to-speech. It reuses everything already built, so it's predictable and verifiable. - **Speech-to-speech realtime models** (single socket, lower latency, support tool calling) are the alternative for Mode 3. The tools stay the same; the verifier still checks the transcript before the answer is shown as text. ## 3. Options landscape (to verify at build time; prices change often) | Need | Options | Notes | |---|---|---| | Avatar video (pre-rendered) | HeyGen API, Synthesia, D-ID, VEED Fabric | HeyGen publishes per-second API rates; Synthesia API access is tied to higher/enterprise tiers | | Live / streaming avatar | HeyGen LiveAvatar, D-ID agents, Tavus | Priced per credit/minute; concurrency limits apply | | Speech-to-speech / realtime voice | OpenAI Realtime (`gpt-realtime`), ElevenLabs agents, Deepgram Voice Agent, Microsoft Voice Live | Support tool calling; compare on latency, interruption handling, languages | | TTS / STT (pipeline) | Any major TTS/STT provider; the browser Web Speech API for prototypes | The mockup uses the browser APIs (no keys, no cost) | Sources: [HeyGen: avatar APIs 2026](https://www.heygen.com/blog/best-ai-avatar-talking-head-apis) · [HeyGen vs Synthesia vs D-ID](https://www.heygen.com/blog/heygen-vs-synthesia-vs-d-id) · [VEED: best avatar APIs](https://www.veed.io/learn/best-avatar-apis) · [Kompozy comparison](https://kompozy.io/ai-video-generation/avatar-video-comparison) · [OpenAI: introducing gpt-realtime](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-realtime/) · [AssemblyAI: realtime API alternatives](https://assemblyai.com/blog/openai-realtime-api-alternatives). Several of these are vendor-authored; treat prices and latency claims as indicative. ## 4. Guardrails specific to voice & video - **Grounding:** narration = verified claims only; scripts that fail verification are not rendered. - **Disclosure:** a visible "AI-generated presenter" label and a watermark on every video; no likeness of real staff without explicit consent; a stock or illustrated presenter by default. - **Accessibility:** captions always on; downloadable transcript; audio descriptions of charts. - **Languages:** narration in the user's language, with numbers formatted for that locale (still verified against the source values). - **Cost control:** cache by (outcome, filters, snapshot, language); render on demand only for popular views; per-session limits for live mode. - **Privacy:** voice audio is not stored by default; transcripts are kept only for the session. ## 5. Phased plan | Phase | Scope | Effort (indicative) | |---|---|---| | 0. Prototype (done in mockup) | Script from verified insights, scenes synced to charts, browser TTS + speech input | — | | 1. Voice explainers | Server-side TTS, streamed audio, captions, 3–5 languages; voice questions via STT → existing pipeline | ~1–2 weeks | | 2. Presenter videos | Avatar API rendering for the 15 outcome overviews per snapshot; CDN caching; disclosure labels | ~2–3 weeks | | 3. Live presenter | Streaming avatar + realtime voice with the same tools; pilot for briefings | ~4+ weeks + vendor review | ## 6. How to evaluate it Comprehension (quick quiz after viewing vs reading), time-to-insight, completion rate, follow-up question rate, verified-number rate in narration (target 100%), latency to first audio, and cost per explainer view.

content.text:
I've updated the mockup and reopened it in your browser. I also wrote up the voice and video plan in `docs/vision_voice_video.md`.

## What changed
- **World Bank styling.** The colours now come from worldbank.org's own stylesheet:

  | Use | Colour |
  |---|---|
  | Header | `#012740` |
  | Brand dark blue | `#002244` |
  | Brand blue | `#009fda` |
  | Primary | `#004370` |
  | Links | `#0071bc` |

  - **Font:** Open Sans. The Scorecard actually uses a licensed font called Andes, with Open Sans as its fallback.
  - **Header:** uppercase navigation, like the live site.
  - **Icons:** coloured by vertical, using the site's scheme (People orange, Prosperity purple, Planet green, Infrastructure red).
- **The chat and the summary are now one panel.** The side chat is gone. A single "Ask the Scorecard" panel sits above the two charts and holds the question box (text or 🎤 voice), **Summarize this view**, **Explain with video**, the suggested questions and the conversation. The two charts now sit side by side, with the map still the default results view.
- **A small stories feed, using real content.** The Scorecard's CMS has 14 FY26 results stories with images. Four appear in a "Results stories" row on the landing page (with "See all"), and each outcome page has a "Related results story" card. Both link to the published stories.
- **A working voice and video concept.** **Explain with video** builds a short scripted walkthrough of the current view, using only checked numbers:
  1. Intro
  2. Headline
  3. Regions
  4. Over time
  5. Ask me

  Each scene changes the chart. For now your browser's built-in voice reads the script, with captions, and a placeholder figure stands in for a presenter. The 🎤 buttons take spoken questions in Chrome or Edge.

The plan sets out three stages:
1. **Voice over charts:** cheap and quick to start.
2. **Pre-made presenter videos:** covering only the 15 outcome overviews, so they can be cached.
3. **A live presenter for spoken Q&A:** later.

The rule throughout is that every number a presenter says must pass the same check as chat answers before any audio or video is made. The plan also covers labelling the presenter as AI-generated, captions, multilingual narration, keeping costs down, a list of possible vendors with sources, and a phased timeline.

## About Q3
This work covers a lot of Q3, but not all of it. They're graded separately, and Q3 asks for things the app doesn't produce:

- **Q3A, the data pipeline, is shared.** The pipeline we build for the app is the same one Q3 needs. We should still write it up as a separate deliverable that someone else could run.
- **Q3B, the 3-slide deck, is a separate piece of work.** It's a PDF or HTML deck for the Managing Director that picks one thematic area and answers *"which areas and countries would you prioritize in a three-year plan, and where are the biggest gaps or opportunities?"*. The app lets people explore the data; the deck has to make an argument and recommend priorities, with at least one strong chart.

The upside is real, though:
- **One pipeline and analysis serves both.** The app already ranks gaps by region and by country.
- **The figures will be consistent** across the app and the deck.
- **The deck can point to the app** for anyone who wants to dig into the numbers.

Energy looks like a strong area for the deck: the FY26 portfolio is at 258M achieved of 512M expected, Eastern & Southern Africa has the largest gap (117M people still to reach), and electricity access in Africa is still low. We can settle that when we get to it.

**Next step:** build the shared data pipeline, since everything else depends on it. Shall I start? I'll need the Anthropic key for the LLM part later. Put it in `.env` yourself rather than pasting it here, so it stays out of the chat logs.

content: We're building the World Bank assessment (Q1 web app plus Q3 pipeline and deck). The design, the clickable mockup on real FY26 data and the voice/video plan are done. Next, I'll build the shared data pipeline once you say go.

How it works

Data. WBG Corporate Scorecard API (results, client context, metadata, stories), loaded by a pipeline into a local database.

Questions. A fast model classifies each message (set filters, analyze, explain, create artifact, clarify, out of scope). Analysis runs typed, read-only queries; answers and artifacts are built only from their results.

Artifacts. Figures, video explainers and briefing decks are generated from verified data. Each one can be exported as a Jupyter notebook that re-downloads the same data from the Scorecard API and reproduces it.

Verified numbers. Every figure links to its source row: 12.1M✓. Untraceable numbers are marked 12M⚠.

content.text:
I rebuilt the indicator page as a chat on the left with an artifacts panel on the right, and reopened the mockup in your browser. I tested it in a headless browser, and I ran a generated notebook against the live API.

**How the indicator page works now**
- **Left, the chat:** messages, quick actions (Summarize, Make a figure, Video explainer, 3-slide briefing, Export notebook), and a text box with a 🎤 voice option. Each generated artifact also shows up in the chat as a card you can click.
- **Right, the artifacts:** tabs that always **start with Overview**, which holds the same two figures as the live Scorecard indicator page (client-context trend, and the results map with its views and filters), as you asked. Asking something like "girls in western africa" or clicking the map changes the Overview.
- **Stories:** removed from this page. They're only on the landing page now.

**What it can generate** (every number shows ✓, meaning it was checked against the data):
- **Figures:** for example "which country in central africa is struggling". This case broke in your screenshot and now works: Central African Republic is at 1% (8.8K of 1.4M), Niger 3%, Togo 8%, and a chart opens alongside.
- **Video explainer:** the scene-by-scene walkthrough, now shown inside the panel.
- **3-slide briefing:** see the next section. You can export it as HTML and print it to PDF.
- **Jupyter notebook:** available from any artifact. It downloads the data from the Scorecard API, cleans it, re-checks it against the values the app showed, rebuilds the figure and saves a CSV. **I ran one for real against the live API: it worked end to end, with 7 of 7 values matching.**

**How this maps to Q3.** It covers a lot, but there are two gaps:
- **Q3A (the pipeline).** The notebook shows a working pull, clean and check process, but each notebook only covers one artifact. The brief asks for a pipeline that handles the data as-is, with documentation another person could run. That's the shared `pipeline/` module we still need to build, with the notebooks as examples alongside it. Q3 also requires the raw extracts or the fetch scripts.
- **Q3B (the deck).** The briefing already follows the requested story for Energy:
  1. Delivery is at 50%, with 253M people still to reach.
  2. Eastern & Southern Africa has the largest gap, at 117M.
  3. A three-year priority list, ranking countries by remaining gap and by need (electricity access).

  The graders will judge the slides on their own merits, though. The submitted deck needs a carefully chosen area, a tested way of scoring priorities, and a polished PDF. I'd generate it with the app and then refine it by hand, rather than submitting whatever the first run produces.

This is a good point to stop changing the design: the main pieces all work in the mockup. I suggest building next, in this order:
1. **Shared data pipeline:** pull every snapshot, region and country, clean the data, save it to DuckDB, and write the documentation.
2. **Django app:** port this mockup, connect the LLM router and tools, and add the server-side number check.
3. **Generation:** build the Q3 deck and the notebooks from the real app.
4. **Evaluation:** a set of 30 test questions, then screenshots, READMEs and packaging.

import json, urllib.request, concurrent.futures as cf, collections
K="251d66a4a60a4f81adcbe6029adb0226"
def get(url, hdr=None):
    r=urllib.request.Request(url,headers={"User-Agent":"Mozilla/5.0",**(hdr or {})}); return json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(r,timeout=120))
meta=json.load(open("../mock/raw26.json"))["meta"]
res=[m["ind_code"] for m in meta if m["ind_type_name"]=="WBG Results"]
def proj(code):
    d=get(f"https://ext.api.worldbank.org/api/Scorecard/getSCResultIndicatorSummary?key=ind_code&value={code}&snapshotfy=2026",{"apikey":K})
    c=[x["name"] for x in d["manifest"]["schema"]["columns"]]; return code,[dict(zip(c,r)) for r in d["result"].get("data_array") or []], d["manifest"].get("total_chunk_count")
PR={}
with cf.ThreadPoolExecutor(8) as ex:
    for code,rows,ch in ex.map(proj,res):
        f=lambda x: float(x) if x not in (None,"") else 0.0
        agg=collections.defaultdict(lambda:{"n":0,"cmt":0.0,"ach":0.0,"exp":0.0,"projects":[]})
        for r in rows:
            if r["sex_disaggregate_code"]!="_T" or r["age_disaggregate_code"]!="_T" or r["disability_disaggregate_code"]!="_T" or r["sub_ind_code"]: continue
            a=agg[r["cntry_code"]]; a["n"]+=1; a["cmt"]+=f(r["sum_tot_net_cmt_amt"]); a["ach"]+=f(r["sum_ind_base_achieved_val"]); a["exp"]+=f(r["sum_ind_base_expected_val"])
            a["projects"].append([r["proj_id"],r["project_name"],f(r["sum_tot_net_cmt_amt"]),r["approval_fy"],r["closing_fy"]])
        PR[code]=dict(agg); print(code,len(rows),"chunks",ch,"countries",len(agg))
# Projects API: active portfolio
allp=[]; start=0
while True:
    d=get(f"https://search.worldbank.org/api/v2/projects?format=json&status_exact=Active&rows=500&os={start}&fl=id,countrycode,countryshortname,totalcommamt,sector1,sector2,sector3,regionname")
    ps=list(d["projects"].values()); allp+=ps; start+=500
    if start>=int(d["total"]) or not ps: break
print("active projects",len(allp))
json.dump({"proj":PR,"active":allp},open("org.json","w"))
pop=get("https://data360api.worldbank.org/data360/data?DATABASE_ID=WB_WDI&INDICATOR=WB_WDI_SP_POP_TOTL&timePeriodFrom=2022&timePeriodTo=2024&top=1000&skip=0")["value"]
P={}
for v in pop:
    if v["REF_AREA"] not in P or v["TIME_PERIOD"]>P[v["REF_AREA"]][0]: P[v["REF_AREA"]]=[v["TIME_PERIOD"],float(v["OBS_VALUE"])]
json.dump(P,open("pop.json","w")); print("pop",len(P))
s=collections.Counter()
for p in allp:
    for k in ("sector1","sector2","sector3"):
        if isinstance(p.get(k),dict) and p[k].get("Name"): s[p[k]["Name"]]+=1
print(s.most_common(25))
EOF

## 12. v0.3: Research agent (cross-organization questions) and artifacts

### 12.1 New router intent: `research`
Strategic questions ("which areas and countries should a three-year plan prioritize…", "where are the biggest
gaps or opportunities…") go to a **research pipeline** instead of the analyze pipeline. They can be asked from the
landing page or inside any outcome workspace.

| Step | What happens | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 0. Scope | If no thematic area is given, **clarify** with outcome-area chips (suggest the one with the best country-level data) | metadata |
| 1. Results | WBG Results by country (achieved, expected, gap, ratio) | Scorecard `getSCSUMMARYDATA` (COUNTRY) |
| 2. Need | Client-context need indicator by country (latest year) | Scorecard client context |
| 3. Population | Population → **people in need** when the need indicator is a % of population | Data360 `WB_WDI_SP_POP_TOTL` |
| 4. Footprint | Projects and commitments contributing to the indicator, plus active projects in the sector | Scorecard `getSCResultIndicatorSummary` + World Bank Projects API |
| 5. Prioritize | Deterministic rules in code: **accelerate** (expected ≥ p60, achieved < 40%) and **expand** (top need, pipeline covers < 25% of need), plus a regional focus and strong performers | computed |
| 6. Write + artifacts | Writer step drafts the answer from step 1–5 outputs (claim-tagged); generates the opportunity matrix, 3-slide briefing and research notebook | — |

- The plan is shown live in the chat (each step ticks off with what it found), as a "thinking out loud" panel.
- **Budget:** up to 12 tool calls; the scoring is **code, not LLM judgement**, so it's reproducible and testable.
- **Caveats are part of the answer:** expected ≠ target; project-level data is World Bank only (not IFC/MIGA);
  sector matching on the Projects API is approximate; coverage vs need is indicative.

| Tool | Returns |
|---|---|
| `get_country_results(ind_code, snapshot)` | all countries: achieved, expected, gap, ratio |

| `get_project_footprint(ind_code)` | per country: # contributing projects, commitments, project list |
| `get_active_portfolio(sector_pattern)` | per country: # active projects, commitments (Projects API) |
| `prioritize(ind_code, rules)` | accelerate / expand / strong lists + regional shares (deterministic) |
| `create_artifact(type, spec)` | figure / video / deck / notebook built from stored tool results |

### 12.3 Artifacts
Every artifact stores the tool results it was built from (with claim IDs). That is what makes the **notebook export**
possible: the notebook re-pulls the same sources, applies the same cleaning and rules, and re-checks the shown values.

content.text:
You can now paste the Q3 question into the landing-page Ask box, and a research agent answers it using data from across the organization. The mockup is open again in your browser.

**How it works**
1. **It asks which area first.** Your question says "your chosen thematic area", so the agent offers the 15 outcome areas as options. It suggests ★ Energy, which has the best country-level data.
2. **It runs a visible plan.** Each step is checked off in the chat with what it found:
   - Scorecard results by country (107 countries)
   - Client-context need, here electricity access (143 countries)
   - Population from Data360, used to estimate people without access
   - Operational footprint: Scorecard project-level commitments, plus active energy projects from the World Bank Projects API
   - Prioritization rules, applied in code rather than left to the LLM's judgement
   - Writing the answer and building the artifacts
3. **It answers with real data.** Every number carries a ✓:
   - **Regional focus: Eastern & Southern Africa.** 57% of people without electricity in client countries live there, and 196M is still to be delivered.
   - **Accelerate delivery** where portfolios are large but behind: Ethiopia (38% of 41.6M), Nigeria (31%), Kenya (34%), Uzbekistan (34%).
   - **Expand the footprint** where need far exceeds the pipeline: DR Congo (84.7M people without access, against 6.4M expected), Niger, Sudan, Angola.
   - **Learn from strong delivery:** India (82%), Pakistan (79%).
   - A collapsible note sets out the method and caveats: "expected" is not a target, project data covers the World Bank only, and sector matching is approximate.
4. **It produces three artifacts:**
   - an **opportunity matrix** plotting need against expected results, with bubble size showing active commitments;
   - a **3-slide briefing** whose third slide is now the accelerate/expand framing;
   - a **research notebook**.

**Tested:** I ran the research notebook against the live Scorecard, Data360 and Projects APIs. It took about 20 seconds and reproduced exactly the same accelerate and expand lists as the app, with every value matching ✓. It also handles a quirk: the Bank's own code for DR Congo is `ZR`, not the ISO code `CD`.

**One caveat:** the generated deck is a strong draft for Q3B, but it isn't the final submission yet. Slide 3 still overflows slightly at the bottom. The prioritization thresholds (top 40% of portfolios by size and below 40% delivered; pipeline covering less than 25% of need) are reasonable defaults that should be stress-tested before we present them to "the MD". We'll polish both when we generate the final deck from the real app.

I've added this to `docs/platform_architecture.md` (v0.3, §12): a new `research` intent, the six-step pipeline, the new tools, and how artifacts store their data so they can be exported as notebooks.

The design now covers Q1 and Q3 end to end in the mockup. I'd suggest we start building. Step 1 is the shared data pipeline, which will pull this exact set of data (Scorecard by snapshot, region, country and project, plus Data360 and the Projects API) into DuckDB, with documentation. Shall I go ahead?

content.text:
Both fixes are in, and I've reopened the mockup in your browser.

**1. Voice questions now get a spoken answer.**
- **How it's triggered:** if you ask with the 🎤 button, on the landing page or in the workspace, the reply is read aloud.
- **What gets read:** a cleaned-up version of the answer. It skips the ✓ marks, the "How I got this" sections and the buttons, and says numbers in words ("38 percent", "41.6 million"). When an artifact is created it says "I've opened the briefing on the right." Long research answers are cut off after the main points, followed by "The full answer is on screen."
- **Stopping it:** a "🔊 speaking · stop" link appears under the input box. Typing a question or clicking a suggestion also stops it and turns voice replies off again.
- **Not tested:** I couldn't play audio in my headless test, so please try a voice question in Chrome and tell me how it sounds.

**2. The deck charts are no longer squashed.**
- **The cause:** each slide used to be laid out at whatever width the panel happened to have, which crushed the charts into about 200px.
- **The fix:** slides are now built at a fixed **1280×720** size, the way slide tools work, and scaled down to fit the panel. The charts are rendered as sharp images at their full size (690×430, at double resolution).
- **Result:** the region chart and the opportunity matrix keep their proportions, and the HTML/PDF export comes out at exactly the size you see.

**Two known limits:**
- **Small text in the panel.** Because each slide is shrunk to roughly half size there, the text is small. The exported deck is full size; an "expand to full screen" button would help in the app.
- **Overlapping labels.** In the No Learning Poverty deck, the countries with no current portfolio (Myanmar, South Africa, Nicaragua) all sit on the bottom edge of the matrix, so their labels overlap. I'll fix that in the real build.

The mockup now covers all the interactions we've discussed: the landing tiles, the research agent, chat with artifacts, the map, voice in and out, video, the deck and notebooks. I'd like to move on to building it:
1. Shared data pipeline into DuckDB.
2. Django app with the LLM router, tools and server-side number checks.
3. Generate the final Q3 deck and notebooks.
4. 30-question evaluation, screenshots, READMEs and the zip.

Shall I start the pipeline?

Two changes:
1. **The agent answers straight away.** The question says "your chosen thematic area", so the agent will make that choice itself instead of stopping to ask. It scans all 15 outcome areas, picks one by a stated rule (the largest remaining gap, among areas with country-level results and need data), explains the choice, and runs the analysis.
2. **You can redirect it by typing.** Typing an area name ("education", "health") on the landing page or in the chat re-runs the research for that area. Chips stay available as shortcuts.

content.text:
**Why it said that.** The text and the chart were measuring two different things, and the wording didn't make that clear:
- **Bar labels (62%, 55%)** are the *delivery rate*: achieved ÷ expected. On that measure Latin America & Caribbean (55%) is lowest, as you say.
- **"Largest remaining gap" in the summary** is an *absolute* number: expected − achieved, in people. Western & Central Africa has the most people still to reach (about 41M) because its portfolio is much bigger than Latin America's (about 10M). It isn't the lowest in percentage terms.

There's a second problem in this chart: Europe & Central Asia is at 255%, which looks like a data quirk. "Furthest along" picked it purely because its ratio is the highest.

In the real build: every statement will name its measure ("lowest delivery rate" vs "most people still to reach"); ratios above 105% will be flagged as data checks rather than ranked as best; and the eval set will include questions that test this distinction.

Now, the build. The Django app reads from the database, so I'll start with the shared data pipeline, then set up the Django project on top of it. First, a look at the environment.

"""Extract: pull every source and store it unchanged (all columns as text) in data/raw/ as Parquet.

Raw files are cached; re-running only fetches what is missing unless ``refresh=True``.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import concurrent.futures as cf
import json
import logging
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

from . import clients, config

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)


def _save(rows: list[dict], path: Path) -> int:
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    df = df.astype("string") if len(df) else df
    df.to_parquet(path, index=False)
    return len(df)


def _cached(path: Path, refresh: bool) -> bool:
    if path.exists() and not refresh:
        log.info("cached  %s", path.relative_to(config.DATA_DIR))
        return True
    return False


def _summary(area_type: str, area_code: str, org: str, fy: int) -> list[dict]:
    rows = clients.scorecard("getSCSUMMARYDATA", refareatype=area_type, refareacode=area_code,
                             orgCode=org, snapshotfy=fy)
    for r in rows:  # keep the request that produced each row (useful for lineage and debugging)
        r.update(query_area_type=area_type, query_area_code=area_code, query_org=org)
    return rows


def extract_snapshot(fy: int, refresh: bool = False, countries_limit: int | None = None) -> None:
    out = config.RAW_DIR / f"fy{fy}"

    for name, endpoint in [("indicators", "getSCMETADATA"), ("sub_indicators", "getSCSubIndicatorMetaData"),
                           ("countries", "getSCCountryDATA")]:
        path = out / f"{name}.parquet"
        if not _cached(path, refresh):
            n = _save(clients.scorecard(endpoint, snapshotfy=fy), path)
            log.info("fetched %s fy%s: %s rows", name, fy, n)

    path = out / "summary.parquet"
    if not _cached(path, refresh):
        countries = pd.read_parquet(out / "countries.parquet")
        codes = sorted(countries["cntry_code"].dropna().unique())[:countries_limit]
        jobs = ([("REGION", r, "ALL") for r in config.REGIONS] + [("FCS", "FCS", "ALL")]
                + [("REGION", "ACW", o) for o in config.INSTITUTIONS] + [("COUNTRY", c, "ALL") for c in codes])
        rows, failed = [], []
        with cf.ThreadPoolExecutor(config.MAX_WORKERS) as ex:
            futures = {ex.submit(_summary, t, c, o, fy): (t, c, o) for t, c, o in jobs}
            for f in cf.as_completed(futures):
                try:
                    rows += f.result()
                except clients.ApiError as exc:
                    failed.append(futures[f])
                    log.warning("summary failed %s: %s", futures[f], exc)
        n = _save(rows, path)
        (out / "summary_failures.json").write_text(json.dumps(failed))
        log.info("fetched summary fy%s: %s rows from %s requests (%s failed)", fy, n, len(jobs), len(failed))

    path = out / "projects.parquet"
    if not _cached(path, refresh):
        meta = pd.read_parquet(out / "indicators.parquet")
        codes = meta.loc[meta["ind_type_name"] == "WBG Results", "ind_code"].tolist()

        def one(code):
            rows = clients.scorecard("getSCResultIndicatorSummary", key="ind_code", value=code, snapshotfy=fy)
            return [{**r, "query_ind_code": code} for r in rows]

        with cf.ThreadPoolExecutor(config.MAX_WORKERS) as ex:
            rows = [r for batch in ex.map(one, codes) for r in batch]
        log.info("fetched projects fy%s: %s rows", fy, _save(rows, path))


def extract_global(refresh: bool = False) -> None:
    out = config.RAW_DIR / "global"
    latest = max(config.SNAPSHOTS)

    path = out / "outcomes.parquet"
    if not _cached(path, refresh):
        cms = clients.scorecard_cms("get_outcomes_indicators", fy=latest)
        _save(cms["outcomes"], path)
        _save(cms.get("indicators") or [], out / "outcome_indicators.parquet")
        log.info("fetched CMS outcomes: %s", len(cms["outcomes"]))

    path = out / "stories.parquet"
    if not _cached(path, refresh):
        rows = clients.scorecard_cms("get_home_narratives", fy=latest)
        for r in rows:
            r["related_outcomes"] = json.dumps(r.get("related_outcomes") or [])
        log.info("fetched CMS stories: %s", _save(rows, path))

    for name, code in config.DATA360_INDICATORS.items():
        path = out / f"data360_{name}.parquet"
        if not _cached(path, refresh):
            log.info("fetched Data360 %s: %s rows", code, _save(clients.data360(code, 2015, latest), path))

    path = out / "active_projects.parquet"
    if not _cached(path, refresh):
        rows = clients.active_projects()
        for r in rows:  # flatten nested fields
            r["countrycode"] = json.dumps(r.get("countrycode") or [])
            for k in ("sector1", "sector2", "sector3"):
                v = r.get(k)
                r[k] = v.get("Name") if isinstance(v, dict) else v
        log.info("fetched active projects: %s", _save(rows, path))


def run(snapshots=None, refresh: bool = False, countries_limit: int | None = None) -> None:
    extract_global(refresh)
    for fy in snapshots or config.SNAPSHOTS:
        extract_snapshot(fy, refresh, countries_limit)

"""Transform: clean the raw extracts into tidy, typed tables.

"""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import re

import pandas as pd

from . import config

RES_KEY = ["snapshot_fy", "ind_code", "sub_ind_code", "org", "area_code", "sex", "age", "disability",
           "joint_programming", "eligibility"]
CTX_KEY = ["snapshot_fy", "ind_code", "sub_ind_code", "area_code", "sex", "age", "disability", "year"]


def _num(s: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    return pd.to_numeric(s.astype("string").str.replace(",", "", regex=False), errors="coerce")


def _raw(fy: int, name: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    return pd.read_parquet(config.RAW_DIR / f"fy{fy}" / f"{name}.parquet")


def _global(name: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    return pd.read_parquet(config.RAW_DIR / "global" / f"{name}.parquet")


def slugify(text: str) -> str:
    return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", text.lower()).strip("-")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- reference tables
def build_areas(snapshots) -> pd.DataFrame:
    frames = [_raw(fy, "countries").assign(snapshot_fy=fy) for fy in snapshots]
    c = pd.concat(frames).sort_values("snapshot_fy").drop_duplicates("cntry_code", keep="last")
    countries = pd.DataFrame({
        "area_code": c["cntry_iso3_code"], "area_type": "COUNTRY", "name": c["cntry_short_name"],
        "iso2": c["cntry_code"], "iso3": c["cntry_iso3_code"], "region_code": c["rgn_wb_code"],
        "region_name": c["rgn_wb_name"], "fcs": c["cntry_fcv_ind"].eq("Y"), "ldc": c["least_dev_cntry_flag"].eq("Y"),
        "income_code": c["cntry_inc_class_code"], "income_name": c["cntry_inc_class_name"],
        "lending": c["cntry_elig_class_code"], "sids": c["cntry_sids_class_flag"].eq("Y"),
        "small_state": c["cntry_small_state_class_flag"].eq("Y")})
    countries = countries.dropna(subset=["area_code"])
    names = (c.dropna(subset=["rgn_wb_code"]).drop_duplicates("rgn_wb_code")
              .set_index("rgn_wb_code")["rgn_wb_name"].to_dict())
    names["ACW"] = "All countries"
    groups = pd.DataFrame([{"area_code": r, "area_type": "REGION", "name": names.get(r, r), "region_code": r}
                           for r in config.REGIONS]
                          + [{"area_code": "FCS", "area_type": "GROUP", "name": "Fragile and conflict-affected situations"}])
    return pd.concat([groups, countries], ignore_index=True)


def iso2_to_area(areas: pd.DataFrame) -> dict:
    m = areas.dropna(subset=["iso2"]).set_index("iso2")["area_code"].to_dict()
    m.update({r: r for r in config.REGIONS}, FCS="FCS")
    return m


def build_outcomes(indicators: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    cms = _global("outcomes")
    out = pd.DataFrame({"outcome_id": cms["outcome_id"].astype(int), "name": cms["outcome_name"],
                        "description": cms["outcome_desc"],
                        "context_description": cms["client_context_description"],
                        "results_description": cms["results_description"]})
    vert = indicators.dropna(subset=["outcome_id"]).groupby("outcome_id")["vertical"].agg(
        lambda s: s.dropna().mode().iat[0] if s.dropna().size else None)
    out["vertical"] = out["outcome_id"].map(vert)
    out["slug"] = out["name"].map(slugify)
    return out.sort_values("outcome_id")


def build_indicators(snapshots) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
    latest = max(snapshots)
    m = _raw(latest, "indicators")
    kind = {"WBG Results": "results", "Client Context": "context", "Vision": "vision"}
    ind = pd.DataFrame({
        "ind_code": m["ind_code"], "name": m["ind_name"], "display_name": m["ind_display_name"].fillna(m["ind_name"]),
        "type": m["ind_type_name"].map(kind), "unit": m["ind_unit_of_measure"],
        "outcome_id": _num(m["ind_outcome_area_code"].str.extract(r"(\d+)")[0]).astype("Int64"),
        "vertical": m["ind_vertical_name"], "definition": m["ind_definition"],
        "long_definition": m["ind_long_definition"], "wdi_code": m["dec_ind_code"],
        "wb": m["ind_wb_flag"].eq("Y"), "ifc": m["ind_ifc_flag"].eq("Y"), "miga": m["ind_miga_flag"].eq("Y"),
        "has_sub_indicators": m["sub_ind_flag"].eq("Y"), "sex_disaggregated": m["ind_sex_disaggregate_flag"].eq("Y"),
        "country_disaggregated": m["ind_cntry_disaggregate_flag"].eq("Y"),
        "scale_type": m["scale_type_code"], "note": m["ind_note"]})
    # "higher is better" is needed to read need indicators correctly (poverty, stunting... are higher = worse)
    worse = r"cannot|poverty|stunt|insecur|risk|hazard|displaced|not in education|distress|inequality|emission|shortfall"
    ind["higher_is_better"] = ~ind["name"].str.contains(worse, case=False, regex=True)
    s = _raw(latest, "sub_indicators")
    sub = pd.DataFrame({"ind_code": s["ind_code"], "sub_ind_code": s["sub_ind_code"], "name": s["sub_ind_name"],
                        "display_name": s["sub_ind_display_name"], "female": s["female_sub_ind"].eq("Y"),

        "snapshot_fy": _num(df["snapshot_fy"]).astype("Int64"), "snapshot_date": pd.to_datetime(df["snapshot_date"]),
        "ind_code": df["ind_code"], "sub_ind_code": df["sub_ind_code"],
        "area_code": df["ref_area_code"].map(area_map), "area_type": df["ref_area_type_code"],
        "sex": df["sex_disaggregate_code"].fillna("_T"), "age": df["age_disaggregate_code"].fillna("_T"),
        "disability": df["disability_disaggregate_code"].fillna("_T")})


def build_results(snapshots, area_map) -> pd.DataFrame:
